clue.text: Fictional detective in horror film

definitions.meaning: first meaning: Mickey Spillane's private eye Mike
second meaning: the British studio famous for gothic chillers

explanation.surface: A private eye turns up as a character in a scary movie.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests one detective inside one film; in fact the two halves name the same word separately, a pulp sleuth's surname and a famous horror studio.
explanation.definitionFit: Mike Hammer is Spillane's hard-boiled private eye, and Hammer Films made the classic British Dracula and Frankenstein pictures.

clue.text: Cry of grief from girl who's lost a son

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: a girl who has lost something no longer has it, so a letter goes missing from her

parts.note: a lass is a girl
S is the standard abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: A young woman, bereaved of her child, cries out in sorrow.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'a girl who's lost son': A plus LASS with one S taken away.
explanation.definitionFit: Alas is an exclamation used to express sorrow, regret or pity, exactly a cry of grief.

clue.text: Minister mends loan bungle

indicators.note: a bungle is a botched, messed-up job, so the words before it are scrambled

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A government minister clumsily fixes up a botched loan.
explanation.walkthrough: Peter Mandelson was a Labour cabinet minister, famously resigning over an undeclared home loan, which makes the surface pointed.
explanation.definitionFit: Peter Mandelson served as a Labour cabinet minister under Blair and Brown, so he is an example of a minister.

clue.text: Roman Catholic's embracing prophet's remains

indicators.note: to embrace is to hug and enclose, so the first part wraps around the second

parts.note: RC is the abbreviation for Roman Catholic, with the S of the possessive
Eli is the Old Testament priest and prophet who raised Samuel

explanation.surface: A Catholic church holds onto the bones of a holy prophet.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-S on 'Roman Catholic's' supplies the final S; the one on 'prophet's' is just surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Relics are physical remains, especially the bones of a saint kept for veneration, or leftovers from the past.

clue.text: Sailor Ray, perhaps, is after singular sea creature

parts.note: S is the grammar abbreviation for singular
a tar is a sailor
a ray is an example of a fish

explanation.surface: A seaman named Ray is chasing an unusual marine animal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ray' looks like a sailor's first name; it is the flat fish. 'is after' places the sailor and fish after the S.
explanation.definitionFit: A starfish is a star-shaped echinoderm living on the seabed, a classic marine animal.

clue.text: Character raising funds for popular hobby

parts.note: stamp means character or kind, as in 'a man of that stamp'
collecting money for a cause is raising funds

explanation.surface: Someone who fundraises for a well-liked pastime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Character' seems to mean a person; it is the other sense, kind or stamp.
explanation.definitionFit: Philately, gathering postage stamps, is among the most widespread pastimes people pursue in their leisure time.

clue.text: Much dismayed, a quiet friend took the initiative

parts.note: taken as written
p (piano) is the musical direction for quiet
a pal is a friend
to lead is to take the initiative

explanation.surface: Someone is horrified when a shy friend takes charge.
explanation.definitionFit: To be appalled is to be shocked and horrified, a strong form of being dismayed.

clue.text: Throw a dance

definitions.meaning: second meaning: the Highland dance of Scotland

explanation.surface: Host a party with dancing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Throw a dance' reads like hosting one; the verb and the noun are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: To fling is to hurl something, and the Highland fling is a lively Scottish solo dance.

clue.text: Perhaps pert Tess is a relative by marriage

indicators.note: perhaps hints that the following words could be a different word in another order

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A cheeky girl called Tess might be an in-law.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' suggests an example, but it signals that the letters may be arranged differently. 'is' appears both as fodder and as the link; the fodder needs its letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A stepsister is the daughter of one's step-parent, related through a parent's remarriage rather than blood.

clue.text: Make animal go into ornamental shrub

indicators.note: make, paired with into, orders that one set of words be turned into something new
into names the transformed result, completing the instruction to remake the words

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Force a creature to wander into the garden bushes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Make X into Y' instructs turning one set of letters into another word.
explanation.definitionFit: Magnolias are flowering trees and bushes grown in gardens for their large showy blooms.

clue.text: Tellytubby is extremely excited and ready for action

parts.note: Po is the smallest, red Teletubby
taken as written

indicators.note: read literally, at the extremes: only the two end letters of the next word are kept

parts.note: the first and last letters of excited

explanation.surface: A children's TV character gets thrilled and set to go.
explanation.walkthrough: The Teletubbies were a BBC toddlers' programme; its four characters were Tinky Winky, Dipsy, Laa-Laa and Po.
explanation.definitionFit: Poised describes someone balanced and prepared, ready to act at a moment's notice.

clue.text: Notes about advocate for Houdini, perhaps

parts.note: E is a musical note, and the plural E's stands for more than one of it
c (circa) is the abbreviation for about
an apologist argues in defence of a cause

explanation.surface: Musical notes describing someone who argues on behalf of the famous magician.
explanation.walkthrough: Houdini was the celebrated escape artist; 'perhaps' marks him as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Harry Houdini was the most famous performer of escapes from chains and locked boxes, an example of the profession.

clue.text: A broken tin, we hear, lets out ethylene glycol

parts.note: taken as written, for rearranging

indicators.note: something broken is smashed apart, so the words around it are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, for rearranging

indicators.note: what we hear is spoken, so the answer only sounds like the synonym

parts.note: to let out is to free

explanation.surface: A cracked can leaks out a chemical.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a leaking tin; ethylene glycol is the main ingredient of engine coolant.
explanation.definitionFit: Ethylene glycol is the chemical used in car radiators to lower the freezing point of the coolant water.

clue.text: Top men heartlessly discuss deaths

indicators.note: to top is to cut off the head, so the first letter of the word goes

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: without its heart, a word keeps only its outside letters

parts.note: the word discuss with all its middle letters gone

explanation.surface: Senior figures talk through mortality figures without feeling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top' is a verb here, to behead: men loses its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: An end is a death, as in 'met his end', so the plural means deaths.

clue.text: Beyond Slough it's cloudy

parts.note: over means beyond, as in over the hill
to slough is to shed, as a snake casts its skin

explanation.surface: Past the town of Slough the weather turns grey.
explanation.walkthrough: Slough looks like the Berkshire town west of London; it is the verb to shed.
explanation.definitionFit: An overcast sky is completely covered with grey cloud, so the two words are synonyms.

clue.text: Bloody Quiptic!

definitions.meaning: first meaning, read as two words: an angry word, an expletive
second meaning: the Quiptic is itself a puzzle of this kind

explanation.surface: A solver's exasperated outburst at this very puzzle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bloody' is a cross word, a swear word; the Quiptic is the Guardian's beginner puzzle.
explanation.definitionFit: Split in two it names an angry swear word such as bloody; whole, it is the grid puzzle the Quiptic exemplifies.

clue.text: Dizzy Di taking the country to heart

indicators.note: taking something in means holding it inside, so one piece is put within another
taken to heart means put right in the middle, where the inserted piece goes

parts.note: taken as written
a Middle Eastern nation

explanation.surface: Princess Diana, scatterbrained, holds her homeland close.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dizzy' looks like a description of Di; it was the nickname of the Victorian prime minister Benjamin Disraeli.
explanation.definitionFit: Benjamin Disraeli, Victorian Conservative prime minister, was widely known by the nickname Dizzy.

clue.text: Every two years Annie and Bill almost get spliced

definitions.note: adverb phrase for an adjective: read as 'happening every two years'

indicators.note: spliced means joined and interwoven, so the two names are mixed together
almost means not quite all, so the final letter of the name is dropped

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A couple, Annie and Bill, nearly marry every couple of years.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get spliced' is slang for getting married, but here it means joining and mixing the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Biennial describes something that occurs once in each two-year period, such as an art festival.

clue.text: Allow access to duck enclosure

parts.note: a duck is a score of nothing in cricket, shaped like O
a pen is an enclosure for animals

explanation.surface: Let someone into the duck pen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Duck' reads as a bird to go in the enclosure; it is the zero.
explanation.definitionFit: To open a door or place is to unlock it and let people come in.

clue.text: Chief fixer

definitions.meaning: second meaning: a bent wire that fastens papers together

explanation.surface: The boss who sorts things out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chief fixer' reads as a head troubleshooter; the two words are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: A staple food is the principal one, and a staple is the small wire fastener that holds sheets together.

clue.text: Perv is a trace mixed up and avoids the truth

indicators.note: things mixed up lose their order, so the words before it are scrambled

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A confused pervert, under investigation, dodges questions.
explanation.definitionFit: To prevaricate is to speak evasively, dodging a straight answer to mislead someone.

clue.text: Instrument for a pansy?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the stringed instrument a little larger than a violin
second meaning: the plant genus that includes pansies and violets

explanation.surface: Which instrument suits a delicate soul?
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the pansy as an example of the plant genus, rather than a person.
explanation.definitionFit: The viola is a bowed string instrument, and Viola is the botanical genus to which garden pansies belong.

clue.text: Badly educated tutee initially getting a second-class mark

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so just the first letters of each word are taken

parts.note: the opening letters of these three words
taken as written

explanation.surface: A poorly taught student receives a mediocre grade.
explanation.definitionFit: Beta is the second letter of the Greek alphabet, used in marking for second-rate work.

clue.text: Far away in an obscure motel

indicators.note: in says the answer sits inside the following words, spanning their letters

parts.note: found running across the two words

explanation.surface: A distant, little-known roadside lodging.
explanation.definitionFit: Remote means distant or isolated, a long way off from other places.

clue.text: I'm dead rude

parts.note: taken as written
dead and proper are both British slang intensifiers meaning very

explanation.surface: A cheerful admission of being thoroughly bad-mannered.
explanation.walkthrough: In British speech 'dead rude' and 'proper rude' both mean very rude.
explanation.definitionFit: Improper behaviour is indecent or unseemly, so rude in the sense of offensive or lewd.

clue.text: Telling of genital disorder after end of affair

indicators.note: the end of a word is its last letter, which is all that is kept

parts.note: the final letter of affair

indicators.note: disorder means confusion, so the word beside it is jumbled

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Describing a medical complaint picked up once a fling ended.
explanation.walkthrough: 'after' puts the rearranged letters after the R.
explanation.definitionFit: To relate a story is to tell or narrate it, so relating means telling.

clue.text: Make stop 'ere, it's said

definitions.note: the clue leans on 'make dear'; endear means to make beloved

parts.note: to stop is to end

indicators.note: it's said means spoken aloud, so the answer is how the phrase sounds

parts.note: 'ere, the dropped-H form of here, sounds like the body part

explanation.surface: A Cockney instruction to halt right here.
explanation.walkthrough: Spoken, 'end 'ere' is the answer; the definition is thin, as endear means to make dear, so 'Make' stands for the whole idea.
explanation.definitionFit: To endear is to cause someone to be loved, literally to render them dear to others.
